messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Since the bombing, Kofi’s life has narrowed. He is a 33-year-old tailor who came to the United States from West Africa several years ago and had built a steady routine in a small alterations shop, taking pride in precise work and long conversations with customers. The attack happened on a crowded downtown afternoon when he had stepped out to deliver a finished suit. He remembers the crack of the blast, the violent shove of air, the screaming, and a rush of people surging in every direction. What remains most vivid is the visual sequence that still comes back to him like a film he cannot stop: a storefront window buckling, a man dropping to the ground, scraps of fabric and ash spinning through the street like something from his own workroom turned grotesque. Other parts are simply gone. When he tries to recall exactly how he got behind a concrete planter or who pulled him up afterward, his mind blanks. At times he can describe the scene in a flat, almost detached way, as if it happened to someone else, and that emotional deadness unsettles him nearly as much as the terror itself.

In the weeks afterward, those odd qualities of memory began to shape how he understood himself. The repeated replay of the blast made him feel trapped in it, while the missing pieces left him unable to reassure himself that he had done what he should have done. He had come to believe that a stronger man would remember clearly, act decisively, know whom to help and when to run. Instead, Kofi was left with the conviction that he was weak and could not trust himself to do the right thing under pressure. The numb, estranged way the memory sometimes returned only deepened that judgment; if his own suffering could feel distant to him, he wondered where exactly he belonged anymore. He began saying, quietly, that he no longer felt at home anywhere—not in the city, not with other immigrants from his community, not even in the shop where he had once felt most like himself.

Those memories also made the world feel constantly poised to rupture again. Entering any space now, Kofi automatically looks for exits before he notices anything else. In his tailoring shop he positions his stool so his back is against the wall and his eyes can track the front door, fitting room curtain, and rear exit at once. If a customer stands between him and the doorway, his body tightens before he has fully registered why. The replayed images of the explosion seem to teach him that disaster arrives without warning, and the gaps in what happened leave him feeling that danger can overtake him before he even understands what is going on. He lives superalert, shoulders tight, listening for changes in sound outside the store.

Over months, that state of watchfulness has pushed him into habits that make immediate sense to him, even as they have shrunk his life. Because he feels unsafe unless he can monitor a room, he avoids restaurants where he cannot choose his seat and turns down invitations if he suspects the place will be crowded. At work he takes fewer walk-in jobs on busy days, telling himself it is about time management when in fact he cannot bear the feeling of being boxed in by people and noise. When his body will not come down from guard, he buries himself in his phone late into the night, scrolling, gaming, clicking from one thing to another so he does not have to sit with what his mind might show him. He has also become more argumentative, picking at small slights with customers or cousins until there is tension in the room; for a few minutes, anger feels easier to manage than dread.

His view of himself drives these strategies as much as the fear does. Because he is certain he is weak and unreliable, Kofi avoids making plans for the future; committing to anything beyond the next few days feels foolish when he no longer trusts his own judgment or believes he can cope if something goes wrong. He tells himself there is no place he truly belongs, and when that thought sharpens, he disappears into screens for hours rather than face how cut off he feels. Sometimes he starts fights almost deliberately, as if proving to himself that closeness will not hold anyway.

The memories continue to feed that cycle. After a replayed scene—glass breaking, bodies dropping, the shock wave hitting his chest—he becomes more restless and more driven to distract himself. The blank spots torment him too; he circles around them mentally, then gives up and opens another game, another video, anything to stop trying to remember. Yet the more time he spends hiding in his phone and avoiding ordinary plans, the smaller and more brittle his life feels, which he takes as further evidence that he has become a lesser version of himself.

By the time he sought help, the cost was showing in concrete ways. He had lost regular customers after snapping at them over minor scheduling changes, and he was spending long evenings alone in his apartment, exhausted but unwilling to sleep. What finally brought him in was a recent moment in the shop when a metal rack crashed to the floor behind him and he dropped into a crouch, heart pounding, unable for several minutes to continue with a hem while the memory ran again in front of him. He is frightened that this is now permanent—that he will always be on guard, always unsure of himself, always cut off from other people. At the same time, he still hopes that if he can understand why his mind keeps taking him back there, he might be able to work, sit in a room, and imagine a future without feeling defenseless.
